body:
## Security Finding

**Severity**: medium
**Type**: unsafe-pattern (update authenticity is never checked on the machine)

Risk: credentials (the fix that works today needs a signing key only the owner can create and store)

Every Tromso image is signed in CI, and `README.md` tells people how to check that by hand. An installed machine never does. Its container policy accepts any image from any registry, so `bootc upgrade` installs whatever `ghcr.io/tuna-os/tromso` returns.

`/etc/containers/policy.json` in the published image (`ghcr.io/tuna-os/tromso:latest`, `sha256:2b89f634081fa2b9221d35af67ba3ba20f3d2ad37a056a6fb38e6d3064e581aa`) is exactly this:

```json
{
    "default": [
        {
            "type": "insecureAcceptAnything"
        }
    ]
}
```

It comes from `elements/tromso/containers-config.bst`, whose description says "insecureAcceptAnything default".

A second copy exists and does not help. `elements/tromso/common.bst` stages the vendored Aurora `files/tromso/aurora-common/system_files/shared/etc/containers/policy.json`, and both elements whitelist the overlap on `/etc/containers/policy.json`, so which file ships depends on staging order. The Aurora copy verifies `ghcr.io/ublue-os` and `quay.io/toolbx-images` against keys under `/usr/lib/pki/containers/` and accepts everything else; it has no entry for `ghcr.io/tuna-os`. The published image carries the bare copy, so those keys and `registries.d` files ship without a policy that uses them.

## Impact

The signature protects nobody who does not run `cosign verify` by hand. Anything that can put an image behind the `:latest` tag reaches every machine as a root filesystem on its next update: a leaked or over-scoped token with `packages: write` on the organization, a compromised job in any repository that can write the package, or a mistake in the rollback workflow, which copies by tag. TLS to GHCR is the only check on the path.

## Recommendation

Option A: Add a key-based signature next to the keyless one and enforce it. The owner creates a cosign key pair and stores the private key as a repository secret; `sign_final` signs with both; the image ships the public key and one `policy.json` with a `sigstoreSigned` rule for `ghcr.io/tuna-os` plus the matching `registries.d` entry. This is the arrangement the vendored Aurora policy already uses for `ghcr.io/ublue-os`. The first image that carries the rule has to be installed by machines that do not check yet.
Option B: Enforce the existing keyless signature with a `fulcio` rule in `policy.json`. No new secret. It only works if the `containers/image` version in this image can match a GitHub Actions workflow identity, which is a URI in the certificate; the documented `fulcio` rule matches an email. I have not confirmed that it can, so this option starts with that check.
Option C: Keep the policy open and say so under "Security Model" in `SECURITY.md`: updates are authenticated by GHCR over TLS, and the cosign signature is for manual verification.

Recommended: A, because it is known to work with the tools already in the image, and the owner-only step is small: `cosign generate-key-pair`, then `gh secret set COSIGN_PRIVATE_KEY -R tuna-os/tromso < cosign.key` and commit `cosign.pub`.

Whichever option is chosen, one element should own `/etc/containers/policy.json`. Today two do, and the result is decided by staging order.

- [ ] `/etc/containers/policy.json` comes from one element
- [ ] (A or B) the shipped policy rejects an unsigned image from `ghcr.io/tuna-os/tromso`, and a test in `tests/pytest/` checks the shipped policy for that rule
- [ ] (C) `SECURITY.md` states what authenticates an update
